body: 6 Min Read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño This visualization compares three ocean data products, sea surface temperature anomaly, apparent visible wavelength, and sea surface height anomaly, over the same months in 2025 and 2026. Signals of El Niño in each map are highlighted with pop-up labels. Credits: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely. El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific. As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there’s an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding. body: A post‑mission comparison of the Orion spacecraft heat shields from Artemis I (left) and Artemis II (right) are shown after removal from their crew modules. Both heat shields are seen rotated for inspection inside the Operations and Checkout Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface. Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected. In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection system effectively safeguarded the crew and Orion systems as the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere. This test flight was the first time astronauts flew aboard Orion.  Orion reached a maximum velocity of 39 times the speed of sound and experienced external temperatures exceeding 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit at its peak, all while the four astronauts inside Orion stayed relatively cool with a cabin temperature in the mid-70 degree Fahrenheit range during their return to Earth from the Moon.   After NASA’s thoro…

body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 15 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The Milky Way over Manhattan Explanation: The city lights outshine the stars in the City That Never Sleeps . Who would have thought that the Milky Way could be visible in this sky? This image was taken with a filter that blocks most visible light , capturing instead only light in the near- infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum (with lower energy than visible light). The astrophotographer’s clever setup blocks most of the light pollution from the city: old incandescent light bulbs and some neon lights are still bright in the near-infrared, but fluorescent and LED light bulbs are not. Of course, stars are also bright in the near-infrared! This image is a reminder that we all live under the same sky , and astronomy allows all of us to learn more about humanity’s place in the Cosmos . title: Carrier heavyweight warns that helping SpaceX could come back to bite the big three
summary: SpaceX's spectrum deal isn't enough to worry this carrier heavyweight.
body: TL;DR T-Mobile’s parent company, Deutsche Telekom, is casting doubt on SpaceX’s ambitions to become the fourth major US wireless carrier. CEO Tim Höttges argues that satellite connectivity can’t replace traditional cellular networks in densely populated areas and that SpaceX faces major infrastructure challenges. Höttges also warned carriers against entering into MVNO agreements with SpaceX, arguing that such partnerships could hurt their own businesses. SpaceX’s major announcement from last week has had the big three US carriers on the defensive. For reference, the Elon Musk-founded company is aiming to become a nationwide competitor to AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon, and it has done so by striking an agreement to acquire spectrum in the 800MHz band. The development should eventually help the company offer reliable indoor coverage. However, there’s a lot that needs to be done before that ambition can come to fruition, and T-Mobile’s parent company, Deutsche Telekom, is making sure SpaceX knows that.
